questions.prompt: A strategy trading one share gained 15% over a year after costs. Over the same year, buying and holding that share gained 20%. What do you conclude about return?
options: The strategy did well, because 15% is a large gain
The strategy and buy and hold did equally well
The strategy should be compared with a different share
The strategy fell 5 percentage points short of doing nothing
questions.explanation: The benchmark is buy and hold on the same share over the same dates. 15% against 20% is 5 points behind it.

questions.prompt: Each round trip costs 0.05% in spread. Why does this matter more for a strategy than for buy and hold?
options: Buy and hold pays a higher spread on each trade
The strategy makes many round trips, and each one pays the spread again
Spreads only apply to strategies, not to holding
The spread is paid once a year by everyone
questions.explanation: Buy and hold buys once and sells once. A strategy with 40 round trips pays the spread 40 times, which cost 1.98% in the example.

questions.prompt: You test a strategy from 2015 to 2020 and measure buy and hold from 2010 to 2020. What is wrong?
options: The dates differ, so the comparison does not measure the same market conditions
Nothing, longer benchmarks are more accurate
Buy and hold must always be measured over one year
The strategy should be tested over more dates than the benchmark
questions.explanation: A benchmark must cover the same dates as the strategy. Different dates include different rises and falls, so the gap would not show the strategy's own skill.
